passages.title: Dengue in Southeast Asia: A Ten-Year Review of Patterns and Prevention
paragraphs: Dengue is a viral infection spread mainly by the Aedes aegypti mosquito and, to a lesser extent, by Aedes albopictus, commonly known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Although most infections cause only a mild fever or no symptoms at all, a small proportion progress to severe dengue, which can be fatal. Because Southeast Asia carries a large share of the global burden, researchers at a university in central Thailand reviewed a decade of regional data to identify when and where the disease strikes and which prevention measures appear to work.

The team analysed national surveillance reports from five countries covering the years 2014 to 2023. Across all five, roughly 70 percent of reported cases occurred between June and October, the months of heaviest rainfall. In Thailand, cases usually began to climb in May and peaked in July. Four serotypes of the virus, labelled DENV-1 to DENV-4, circulate in the region. Infection with one gives lifelong protection against that serotype only, and a later infection with a different serotype raises the risk of severe illness.

The review also points to a shift in who is falling ill. Dengue was long regarded as a childhood disease, yet the median age of patients in Thai surveillance data rose from 12 years in 2014 to 19 years in 2023, a change the authors attribute partly to falling birth rates. Location matters, too: incidence in fast-growing urban districts was 1.6 times higher than in rural districts, reflecting the crowded housing and water containers in which Aedes mosquitoes thrive.

To find out where mosquitoes breed, the researchers drew on household surveys of 1,500 homes in northeastern Thailand. Larvae were most often found in water storage jars, which accounted for 42 percent of positive containers, followed by discarded tyres at 18 percent and flower vases at 11 percent. Infestation was measured with the Breteau index, the number of containers with larvae per 100 houses; a value above 50 was treated as a sign of high outbreak risk.

Several prevention methods were compared. Community clean-up campaigns cut the Breteau index by about a third within two months, but the effect faded once the campaigns ended. Adding temephos sand granules to water jars, or keeping guppy fish in them to eat the larvae, gave longer-lasting results where households kept up the practice. The strongest evidence came from releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia, a bacterium that stops the virus from multiplying inside the insect; a randomised trial in an Indonesian city reported a fall of roughly three quarters in confirmed cases.

The authors conclude that no single tool is enough. They recommend integrated vector management, which combines removing breeding sites, biological control and community education, supported by early-warning systems that use rainfall and temperature data to predict outbreaks several weeks ahead. Newly licensed vaccines may help, they note, but cannot replace the routine work of emptying and covering water containers.

passages.title: Medicine's Newest Assistant Has an Old Problem
paragraphs: A doctor in a busy clinic photographs a patient's mole with a smartphone, and within seconds an app reports that the mark is almost certainly harmless. For many patients, that reassurance will be accurate. For some, however, it may be far less trustworthy than it appears. Artificial intelligence promises to make diagnosis faster, cheaper and more consistent, yet a growing body of evidence suggests that these tools do not serve all patients equally well.

The root of the problem lies in how such systems learn. A skin-lesion classifier is trained on thousands of labelled photographs and becomes skilled at recognising whatever they contain. Reviews of the public image collections used to build dermatology tools have repeatedly found that only a small fraction of the pictures show darker skin. A system trained largely on light skin may therefore miss a melanoma on brown or black skin, not because it was designed to discriminate but because it was never shown enough examples.

Bias can also creep in through the choice of what an algorithm is asked to predict. A widely discussed 2019 study examined software used by American hospitals to decide which patients should receive extra support. The program used past healthcare spending as a proxy for medical need, on the reasonable-sounding assumption that sicker people cost more to treat. But because less money had historically been spent on Black patients with the same conditions, partly owing to unequal access to care, the software judged them to be healthier than they really were. Race was never one of its inputs.

Hardware is not immune either. Pulse oximeters, the small clips that estimate blood oxygen by shining light through a fingertip, have been shown to overestimate oxygen levels in people with darker skin. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when such readings helped determine who was admitted to hospital, the flaw was more than a technical footnote. As these readings are increasingly fed into automated warning systems, a small error at the bedside can be quietly multiplied.

The issue is not confined to the United States or to questions of race. Many AI products used in Asian hospitals are developed abroad, and a model trained on chest X-rays from well-equipped city hospitals may stumble when it meets images from older machines in a rural district hospital in Thailand, or patients with diseases such as tuberculosis that were rare in its training data.

None of this means that medical AI should be abandoned. It does mean that developers should build more representative datasets and report how well a tool performs for each patient group rather than simply on average. Hospitals, for their part, should test imported systems on their own patients before relying on them, and keep monitoring them afterwards. An algorithm can be enormously useful, but only if someone has checked that it works for everyone it is meant to serve.

passages.title: Homework: Help or Hindrance?
paragraphs: Every evening in homes across Thailand, a familiar scene unfolds. A seven-year-old sits at the kitchen table with a pile of worksheets, a tired parent hovers nearby, and an argument is never far away. By the time the last page is finished, it is well past the child's bedtime. I have watched this ritual for years, first as a primary school teacher and now as a parent, and I have come to a firm conclusion: for young children, most homework does more harm than good.

The research supports this view more strongly than many people realise. Large reviews of studies, some dating back to the 1980s, have found that the link between homework and achievement is weak in primary school and becomes noticeably stronger only in the later secondary years. A widely quoted rule of thumb suggests about ten minutes of homework per night for each grade level, which would mean twenty minutes for a second-grader. Yet in a survey of 800 parents in three Thai provinces last year, many reported that their young children spend more than an hour on assignments each evening.

Defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline and responsibility. That is a fair point, but it assumes that children learn those qualities from worksheets rather than from, say, looking after a pet, helping to cook dinner or practising a musical instrument. In reality, the discipline that homework teaches is often the parent's, not the child's. When a task is too difficult to complete alone, it becomes a test of the family's resources: children whose parents have time, education or money for tutors pull further ahead, while others fall behind. Homework, in other words, can quietly widen the very gaps that schools are supposed to close.

There is also a cost that rarely appears in test scores. Childhood is short, and the hours after school are precious. Free play, physical activity and sleep are not luxuries; they are essential to healthy development. Sleep experts generally recommend nine to twelve hours a night for children aged six to twelve, a target that becomes impossible when homework stretches late into the evening.

None of this means that homework should be abolished altogether. For older students, carefully designed assignments can consolidate what has been learned in class and prepare them for independent study at university. Good homework is short, has a clear purpose and receives prompt feedback from the teacher. Busywork that is set merely because parents expect it, or because the timetable says so, should be scrapped.

For younger children, I would go further: replace worksheets with twenty minutes of reading for pleasure, ideally alongside a parent or grandparent. It costs nothing, it builds vocabulary and it turns the evening into something a family can enjoy rather than endure. Surely that is a better use of a child's evening than another page of sums.

passages.title: Village Health Volunteers and Hypertension Control in Rural Northeastern Thailand
paragraphs: Background. Hypertension is one of the leading risk factors for stroke, heart attack and chronic kidney disease, and national surveys suggest that roughly one in four Thai adults is affected. The burden is especially heavy in rural areas, where many people with high blood pressure are unaware of their condition and many of those who are diagnosed do not achieve adequate control. Long distances to hospitals, shortages of doctors and nurses, and a traditional diet high in salt all contribute to this gap.

Thailand, however, possesses a resource that many countries lack: a network of more than one million village health volunteers, known in Thai as Or Sor Mor, who have supported primary care since the late 1970s. Volunteers traditionally assist with health promotion, disease surveillance and home visits, but their role in managing chronic disease has rarely been tested rigorously. The present study therefore aimed to evaluate whether a structured, volunteer-led programme could lower blood pressure among adults with uncontrolled hypertension in rural northeastern Thailand.

Methods. A cluster randomised trial was conducted in 24 villages in one district of a northeastern province between 2023 and 2024. Villages, rather than individuals, were randomly assigned to the intervention or control group, 12 villages in each, to prevent volunteers from sharing advice between neighbours in different arms of the study. A total of 600 adults aged 40 to 75 years with uncontrolled hypertension, defined as a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher despite treatment, were enrolled. People with severe kidney disease, a recent stroke or pregnancy were excluded.

In the intervention villages, 36 volunteers received three days of training in blood pressure measurement, medication counselling and salt reduction. Each volunteer then visited 8 to 10 participants at home every month for 12 months, measuring blood pressure with an automated device, checking that medicines were being taken as prescribed and offering practical advice on cooking with less salt, including reducing the use of pla ra, a fermented fish product common in northeastern dishes. Participants whose readings exceeded 180/110 mmHg were referred immediately to the sub-district health-promoting hospital. Control villages received usual care. The primary outcome was the change in systolic blood pressure after 12 months.

Results. Of the 600 participants, 562 (93.7 percent) completed the follow-up. Mean systolic blood pressure fell by 14.2 mmHg in the intervention group compared with 6.1 mmHg in the control group, a difference of 8.1 mmHg that was statistically significant. By the end of the study, 58 percent of participants in intervention villages had their blood pressure under control, compared with 34 percent in control villages. Self-reported medication adherence also improved more in the intervention group, and estimated daily salt intake declined modestly. No serious adverse events related to the programme were recorded.

Discussion. The reduction observed is comparable to that reported in trials of community health workers in other low- and middle-income countries and, if sustained, would be expected to lower the risk of stroke considerably. A key strength of the programme is that it builds on an existing workforce rather than creating a new one; the additional cost, mainly for training and blood pressure monitors, was estimated at about 450 baht per participant per year. Volunteers also reported that the training increased their confidence and standing in the community.

Limitations and implications. Several limitations should be noted. Neither participants nor volunteers could be blinded to group allocation, and medication adherence was self-reported, which may have exaggerated improvements. The study was carried out in a single district, so the findings may not apply to urban settings or other regions, and 12 months is too short to show effects on strokes or heart attacks. Nevertheless, the results suggest that village health volunteers could play a larger role in chronic disease care. Larger trials with longer follow-up are needed before the model is adopted nationally.

passages.title: Is Thursday the New Friday?
paragraphs: For most of the past century, the five-day, forty-hour week has been treated as a fixed feature of working life. Yet it is a relatively recent invention. Many factory workers in the nineteenth century laboured six days a week, and the two-day weekend spread widely only in the twentieth century, after decades of campaigning by trade unions and experiments by employers who found that rested workers were more productive. Today, a growing number of organisations are asking whether the time has come to take the next step.

The model attracting most attention is often summarised as "100-80-100": employees receive 100 percent of their pay for working 80 percent of their previous hours, in exchange for a commitment to maintain 100 percent of their output. The idea is not simply to squeeze five days of work into four longer ones. Instead, companies are expected to cut wasted time, such as unnecessary meetings, constant email checking and poorly organised projects.

Early results have been encouraging. Public-sector trials of shorter working weeks in Iceland between 2015 and 2019, involving more than 2,500 workers, found that productivity was maintained or improved in most workplaces while staff reported less stress. In a large trial in the United Kingdom in 2022, the great majority of around 60 participating companies chose to continue with the shorter week after the six-month pilot ended. Closer to home, a software company in Bangkok with 80 employees introduced a four-day week last year and reports that staff turnover has fallen sharply.

Supporters point to benefits beyond the office. With an extra day off, employees have more time for family, exercise and rest, and some studies have recorded improvements in sleep and mental health. Employers, meanwhile, find that the promise of a shorter week helps them attract and keep talented staff in competitive labour markets. Reduced commuting may even lower carbon emissions.

Critics, however, warn that the results may not be as transferable as they appear. Companies that volunteer for trials are likely to be those already confident that the change will work. Moreover, the model fits office-based knowledge work far more easily than jobs such as nursing, teaching or retail, where output depends on someone being physically present. A hospital cannot simply close its wards on Fridays; it would need to hire more staff to cover the missing day, raising costs.

For now, the four-day week appears less like a universal solution than a promising option for particular kinds of organisations. Its success depends not on the number of days in the calendar but on whether managers are willing to rethink how work is actually done.

passages.title: Living With Two Languages: Inside the Bilingual Brain
paragraphs: People who speak two languages do not simply switch one off when they use the other. According to a growing body of research, both languages remain active in the brain at the same time, competing for attention even when only one is being spoken. A new study by researchers at a university in Malaysia adds fresh detail to this picture and, its authors argue, helps explain why the effects of bilingualism on thinking have proved so difficult to pin down.

The team used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which tracks changes in blood flow as an indicator of brain activity, to scan 140 adults while they named pictures. Half spoke both Malay and English fluently and used both every day; the rest spoke only Malay. When bilingual participants were told to name objects in one language, regions in the frontal lobe associated with attention and self-control showed increased activity, apparently to suppress the language that was not needed.

This constant juggling, the researchers suggest, may function as a kind of mental exercise. Previous studies have reported that lifelong bilinguals tend to show symptoms of dementia several years later than comparable monolinguals, a finding often explained by the idea of cognitive reserve: a brain that has been exercised more can tolerate more damage before problems become visible. "Managing two languages every day may train the same control systems we use for many other tasks," said Dr. Nurul Aisyah Rahman, who led the study.

However, the evidence for a broader "bilingual advantage" is far from settled. Several large studies, some involving thousands of children, have failed to find that bilinguals outperform monolinguals on tests of attention and task-switching. Critics also point out that bilinguals often differ from monolinguals in other respects, such as education, income or immigration history, which can confound comparisons. In the Malaysian study, the two groups were matched for age and years of schooling, but the authors acknowledge that other differences may remain.

Perhaps the clearest message from the research is a practical one. Whether or not bilingualism sharpens general thinking skills, there is no evidence that learning a second language harms children's development, a fear that once led some teachers to discourage families from speaking their home language. For countries such as Thailand, where many children grow up speaking a regional language or dialect at home and Standard Thai at school, the findings offer reassurance that the two can coexist.
The researchers now plan to follow the same participants for five years to see whether their patterns of brain activity predict changes in memory as they age.

passages.title: The Doctor on Your Wrist
paragraphs: Ten years ago, a device that counted steps was regarded as a gadget for fitness enthusiasts. Today, millions of people wear watches and rings that track their heart rate, sleep, blood oxygen and even the electrical activity of the heart. Manufacturers increasingly market these devices not merely as lifestyle accessories but as tools for health, and some doctors now ask patients to bring their data to appointments.

The potential benefits are real. Several smartwatches can detect an irregular heart rhythm that may indicate atrial fibrillation, a condition that often causes no symptoms but greatly increases the risk of stroke. Because it can come and go, atrial fibrillation is easily missed during a brief clinic visit, whereas a device worn around the clock may capture an episode. For people with diabetes, continuous glucose monitors, small sensors attached to the skin, have reduced the need for painful finger-prick tests and allow treatment to be adjusted in real time.

Yet the same constant monitoring can create problems. Studies of large groups of users have found that a substantial share of people who receive an irregular-rhythm alert are not found to have atrial fibrillation on further testing. Each false alarm can lead to anxiety, extra tests and appointments, adding to the workload of already busy clinics. Some doctors have begun to describe a new type of patient: the healthy person made worried by a stream of numbers they do not fully understand.

Accuracy is another concern. Most consumer devices are not approved as medical instruments, and their readings can vary with skin tone, tattoos, movement and how tightly the device is worn. The popular target of 10,000 steps a day, meanwhile, originated not in medical research but in a marketing campaign for a Japanese pedometer in the 1960s. Recent studies suggest that, for older adults in particular, the benefits of walking begin to level off at a lower number.

There are also questions about who owns the data. Information about a person's heart rate, sleep and location can reveal a great deal, and it is not always clear how companies store it or with whom they share it. In some countries, insurers have offered discounts to customers who share their activity data, raising fears that people who cannot or will not do so could eventually pay more.

None of these concerns means that wearables should be dismissed. Used thoughtfully, and interpreted with the help of a health professional, they can encourage healthier habits and catch problems early. The challenge for doctors and regulators is to make sure that the devices inform patients without overwhelming them.

passages.title: A Nation of Grandparents
paragraphs: In a village outside Roi Et, 71-year-old Bunma Srisuk rises before dawn to tend her vegetable garden, cook breakfast for her two grandchildren and walk the pair to school. Her son and daughter-in-law work in a factory near Bangkok and come home only for the Songkran holiday. Arrangements like hers, in which grandparents raise children whose parents have migrated for work, have become so common that researchers have a name for them: skipped-generation households.

Bunma's situation reflects one of the most rapid demographic transitions in the world. Thailand is widely described as one of the fastest-ageing societies in Southeast Asia, and people aged 60 and over now make up roughly a fifth of the population. Two forces lie behind this change. Thais are living considerably longer than they did half a century ago, thanks to better nutrition, sanitation and health care, and they are having far fewer children. In the 1960s, the average woman gave birth to around six children; today, the figure is well below the level of about two needed to keep a population stable.

The speed of this shift distinguishes Thailand from countries such as Japan, which had already become wealthy by the time its population aged. Economists often warn that Thailand risks growing old before it grows rich. A smaller working-age population means fewer people paying taxes and contributing to pension funds, at precisely the moment when spending on health care is expected to rise. Many older Thais, particularly those who spent their lives working in agriculture or informal jobs, have little or no pension and depend on their children or on a modest monthly government allowance.

Health is a central concern. Chronic conditions such as hypertension, diabetes and dementia become more common with age, and the number of older people who are bedridden or unable to care for themselves is projected to grow. Traditionally, such care has been provided by daughters and daughters-in-law. Yet smaller families, migration to cities and the rising number of women in paid work mean that this source of support is shrinking.

Communities have begun to respond. Many villages have elderly clubs, which organise exercise sessions, health checks and craft activities. Under a community-based long-term care scheme, trained caregivers visit dependent older people at home, while village health volunteers help to monitor their condition. Some local governments have also opened day-care centres, where older residents can spend time together while their families are at work.

Experts argue that deeper changes will be needed, from raising the retirement age and expanding savings schemes to designing homes and public transport that older people can use safely. They also stress that an ageing population is not only a burden. Many people in their sixties and seventies, like Bunma, remain active contributors to their families and communities. The challenge for Thailand is to make sure that longer lives are also healthier and more secure ones.

passages.title: An Invisible Ingredient: Plastic Particles in the Human Body
paragraphs: Since mass production began in the 1950s, plastic has become one of the defining materials of modern life. Its durability, the very quality that makes it so useful, is also the source of a problem that scientists have only recently begun to appreciate. Rather than disappearing, discarded plastic breaks down into ever smaller fragments. Particles smaller than five millimetres are classed as microplastics, while those below one micrometre are usually termed nanoplastics. Over the past decade, attention has shifted from the presence of these particles in oceans and soils to a more personal question: how much of this material is inside us, and what is it doing there?

The routes of exposure are numerous. Microplastics have been detected in drinking water, seafood, salt and honey. A 2024 analysis using a laser-based imaging technique reported hundreds of thousands of plastic particles in a typical litre of bottled water, the great majority of them nanoplastics that earlier methods could not detect. Food and drink are not the only sources. Synthetic clothing sheds fibres into indoor air, and particles worn from car tyres are carried by wind and rain into the wider environment. Indoor dust, which we inhale and which young children often swallow, may be among the most important sources of all.

Once these particles enter the body, some appear to remain there. Researchers have reported microplastics in human blood, lung tissue, the placenta and breast milk, as well as in liver, kidney and brain samples collected at autopsy. Particles in the placenta are of particular concern because they suggest that exposure may begin before birth. Their presence in so many tissues indicates that at least the smallest particles can cross biological barriers once thought to keep them out, including the wall of the gut.

Whether this presence causes harm is much less clear. Laboratory studies on cells and animals have shown that plastic particles can trigger inflammation and oxidative stress, a chemical imbalance that damages cells. Plastics also contain additives such as bisphenol A and phthalates, some of which are known to interfere with hormones. Human evidence is scarcer, but it is beginning to accumulate. In one widely reported 2024 study of patients undergoing surgery to clear fatty deposits from neck arteries, those whose removed plaque contained microplastics were considerably more likely to suffer a heart attack or stroke, or to die, over the following three years.

Such findings must be interpreted with caution. An association of this kind does not prove that plastic caused the harm; people with higher exposure may differ in diet, income or occupation in ways that also affect their health. Measuring microplastics is also technically demanding. Particles are everywhere, including in laboratory air and on the equipment used to collect samples, so contamination can easily inflate results, and methods differ between laboratories, making estimates hard to compare. A widely publicised claim that the average person swallows a credit card's worth of plastic every week, for instance, has since been criticised by other researchers as a substantial overestimate.

Scientists are therefore working to standardise their techniques. Spectroscopic methods, which identify a particle's chemical make-up from the way it absorbs or scatters light, allow researchers to confirm that a fragment is plastic rather than, say, a cotton fibre. Laboratories increasingly run blank samples alongside real ones to measure background contamination, and long-term studies are being designed to link exposure to health outcomes more reliably.

In the meantime, a precautionary approach seems sensible. Individuals can reduce their exposure by not heating food in plastic containers, drinking tap water where it is safe, and ventilating and vacuuming their homes regularly. Yet individual choices can achieve only so much while plastic production continues to grow. Negotiations on a global plastics treaty, which began in 2022, have proved slow and divisive, with countries disagreeing over whether to limit production or focus on waste management. Until the science matures, plastic inside the human body is best regarded not as proof of harm, but as a warning that should not be ignored.

passages.title: The Essay That Wrote Itself
paragraphs: When a lecturer at a university in Chiang Mai marked her students' end-of-term essays last year, she noticed something odd. Many were fluent, well organised and almost free of grammatical errors, yet several cited journal articles that did not exist. The explanation soon became clear: students had used generative AI tools to write all or part of their work, and the software had invented references that looked convincing but led nowhere. Her experience is far from unique. Since chatbots able to produce essays in seconds became freely available in late 2022, universities everywhere have been forced to reconsider what counts as honest work.

The first response of many institutions was to look for a technological fix, and software that claims to detect AI-generated text was quickly adopted. However, such tools have proved unreliable. They can be fooled by simple paraphrasing, and they sometimes flag genuine human writing as machine-generated. A 2023 study found that several popular detectors frequently misclassified essays by non-native speakers of English, whose simpler vocabulary and sentence patterns resemble those typical of AI. For students in countries such as Thailand, the risk of a false accusation is therefore far from trivial.

As a result, many universities have shifted their attention from detection to assessment design. Some have reintroduced handwritten examinations or short oral examinations, in which students must explain and defend their work in person. Others ask students to submit drafts, notes and outlines, so that teachers can see how an assignment developed over time. Tasks are also being redesigned to draw on local data, recent class discussions or students' personal experience, which general-purpose AI tools find harder to imitate.

Not all educators see AI purely as a threat. A growing number argue that, since graduates will use these tools in their careers, universities should teach students to use them responsibly rather than ban them outright. In such courses, students may use AI to brainstorm ideas or check grammar, provided that they declare how they used it and take responsibility for the accuracy of the final text. "Prohibiting the tools entirely would be like banning calculators from a statistics class," said one education researcher at a university in Bangkok.

Clear rules are essential to this approach. Surveys suggest that many students are genuinely unsure where the boundary lies: is it acceptable to ask a chatbot to improve the flow of a paragraph, or to summarise a reading? Without guidance, practices vary from one course to the next, and students who act in good faith can be penalised. Several Thai universities have begun issuing policies that distinguish between permitted, restricted and prohibited uses, although enforcement remains uneven.

Ultimately, the debate goes beyond cheating. It forces educators to ask what they actually want students to learn. If a task can be completed entirely by a machine, it may never have been measuring the thinking skills it was designed to assess.

options: AI detectors are now accurate enough to stop most cheating.
